summary: Almost all views come from Instagram, where the Hindi videos get a few hundred views each, while YouTube Shorts barely reaches anyone (mostly under 30 views). The best video, the PIR motion sensor one, did much better than the rest because it names a familiar device and opens with a surprising claim. Many other videos get views but almost no shares or saves, and the newest ones are still very small, so the data is early and not conclusive.
winningPattern: Everyday device you meet in real life (motion sensor, street light) + a surprising 'it can't actually do X, so how?' hook in Hinglish + a question-style title ending with 🤔 #shorts, posted mainly on Instagram Reels. The top video (PIR) opens with a shock claim ('Motion Sensor Aapko Dekhta Nahi!'). Videos about a familiar everyday object that people can relate to, like the street light, also earned shares and saves, while generic technical titles ('Smoke Detector Fire Kaise Sense Karta Hai?') and robot/IR-sensor topics got little.
doMore: Open with a bold, slightly shocking claim that contradicts what people assume, then answer it (like 'Dekhta Nahi!').
Pick sensors people see daily (lights, doors, taps, phones) and name that object in the title.
Post Instagram Reels first, since that is where nearly all views, shares and saves come from.
End each video with a clear reason to save or share, like 'Save karo, exam mein kaam aayega' or 'Dost ko bhejo jo ye nahi jaanta'.
Post a follow-up to the PIR video, since it is the proven winner, and test the same hook style on 2-3 more topics before changing anything.
stopDoing: Stop making near-duplicate topics (two smoke detector videos, two IR sensor videos) that split the audience.
Stop expecting YouTube Shorts to grow with the same upload; fix the hook and title for it separately or deprioritize it.
Stop using plain textbook titles without a surprise or a question that creates curiosity.
